Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. For every product-measurable kernel $a\in L^2(D\times D;\mathbb C)$, the formula $T_av(x)=\int_Da(x,y)v(y)dy$ defines a representative-independent complex-linear map $L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\|T_a\|\le\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D)}$. Consequently, under [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$,
$$\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\|G_k(\cdot-\cdot)q(\cdot)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\,\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$
For $|D|=0$ the operator is zero.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. If $\rho:=\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}<1$, then for every $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ the equation $u=f+K_ku$ has a unique solution. For each integer $m\ge0$, define the Born partial sum $u_m:=\sum_{j=0}^{m}K_k^jf$. Then
$$\|u-u_m\|_2\le\frac{\rho^{m+1}}{1-\rho}\|f\|_2.$$
No compactness, analytic continuation, or physical uniqueness hypothesis is used in this small-norm branch.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: The integral operator depends linearly on $q$, so $K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}=K_{q-q',k}$ for any $q,q'\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$. By [F2], $\|K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}\|\le C_D\|q-q'\|_\infty$. The operator-norm triangle inequality then gives $|\rho_k(q)-\rho_k(q')|\le C_D\|q-q'\|_\infty$. Thus $q\mapsto\rho_k(q)$ is continuous, $\mathcal U_{D,k}=\{\rho_k<1\}$ is open, and $0\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ because $K_{0,k}=0$.

By [F3], $f_{k,d}(x)=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ belongs to $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and has norm $\sqrt M$. Since $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, [F4] applies with $f=f_{k,d}$ and gives exactly one $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$.

By [F7], $qu_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D)$ with norm at most $\|q\|_\infty\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2$, while [F3] puts $e^{ik\theta\cdot y}$ in $L^2(D)$. Their pairing in [F5] is the stated integral, so it is absolutely convergent and independent of the representatives. Cauchy–Schwarz gives its absolute value at most $\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2$.

By [F7], $\|q\|_2\le\sqrt M\|q\|_\infty$; pairing $|q|$ with $1_D$ in [F5] then gives $\int_D|q(y)|\,dy\le M\|q\|_\infty$. Hence $q_0\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. By [F6], its transform is finite and representative-independent. Since $e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}e^{ikd\cdot y}=e^{-2\pi i y\cdot(k(\theta-d)/(2\pi))}$, the Fourier and integral formulas for $\mathcal B_kq$ agree and are well-defined. This proves the assertion for both data families.

Apply [F8] to $v=u_{q,k,d}$, whose existence is established in step 1.2. It supplies continuity in observation direction and the stated uniform outgoing-wave limit estimate, so the defined data are the physical far-field amplitude for this volume branch.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For any $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, [F8] gives $|e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}e^{ikd\cdot y}|=1$ and [F9] gives $\int_D|h|\le M\|h\|_\infty$. The integral definition therefore yields $|\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)|\le M\|h\|_\infty/(4\pi)$. By [F5] and the Fourier formula in [F1], this integral is the stated Born functional. It is complex-linear in $h$, hence bounded and real-linear for every fixed pair of directions.
Let $f=f_{k,d}$. By the definition and [F8], $|f|=1$ on $D$, so $\|f\|_2=\sqrt M$. The case $N=0$ of [F3] gives $\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2\le\rho\sqrt M/(1-\rho)$.

Subtracting the integral formulas in [F1] yields $\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)\bigl(u_{q,k,d}(y)-f(y)\bigr)\,dy.$ By [F9], $q(u_{q,k,d}-f)$ has $L^2$ norm at most $\|q\|_\infty\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2$. The same unit-modulus calculation as step 1.2, with $d$ replaced by $\theta$, gives $\|e^{ik\theta\cdot(\cdot)}\|_2=\sqrt M$. By [F4], the integral's absolute value is at most $\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2/(4\pi)$; then [F3] and step 1.2 give the first bound, uniformly in the directions.

By [F2], $\rho\le C_D\|q\|_\infty$. When $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, monotonicity of $t\mapsto t/(1-t)$ on $[0,1)$ gives $\rho/(1-\rho)\le C_D\|q\|_\infty/(1-C_D\|q\|_\infty)$. Substitution into step 2.1 proves the second bound.

For nonzero $q$ with $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, divide the second bound by $\|q\|_\infty$; the quotient is at most $\frac{M C_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}$, which tends to zero as $\|q\|_\infty\to0$. Since [F10] makes zero an interior point, the bounded real-linear map from step 1.1 satisfies the Fréchet remainder criterion [F7], with the Banach-space hypotheses in [F6]. Also $\mathcal S_k(0)=0$ by its definition. Thus $D\mathcal S_k(0)(\theta,d)h=\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)$ for each fixed pair, with the same remainder estimate uniformly over the full direction family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set with $0<M:=|D|<\infty$, and let $k>0$. Write $S^2:=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:|v|=1\}$ and $C_D:=\sqrt{M\,\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$. For $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, extended by zero off $D$, set $G_k(z):=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ and $G_k(0):=0$, and let
$$K_{q,k}v(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \rho_k(q):=\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2(D)\to L^2(D)}.$$
The **small-norm contrast class** is
$$\mathcal U_{D,k}:=\{q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C):\rho_k(q)<1\}.$$
For $d\in S^2$, put $f_{k,d}(x):=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ on $D$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, let $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ denote the unique solution of $u=f_{k,d}+K_{q,k}u$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, define the exact far-field data family by
$$\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)u_{q,k,d}(y)\,dy,\qquad (\theta,d)\in S^2\times S^2.$$

For $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, define its first Born data by
$$\mathcal B_k h(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}h(y)e^{ikd\cdot y}\,dy=\frac1{4\pi}\widehat{h_0}\!\left(\frac{k}{2\pi}(\theta-d)\right),$$
where $h_0$ is the zero extension of $h$ to $\mathbb R^3$ and $\widehat g(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ for $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. No uniqueness or stability outside $\mathcal U_{D,k}$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and notation of the fixed-frequency far-field definition. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ put $\rho=\rho_k(q)$. Uniformly over all incident and observation directions,
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M}{4\pi}\|q\|_\infty\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.$$
Whenever $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, this implies
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M C_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty^2}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}.$$
For each fixed $(\theta,d)$, the scalar map $q\mapsto\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)$ on the open domain $\mathcal U_{D,k}$, with $L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\mathbb C$ viewed as real Banach spaces, is Fréchet differentiable at $q=0$ and has derivative $h\mapsto\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)$. The remainder bound is uniform in $(\theta,d)$; it asserts no nonlinear uniqueness or stability result.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have singular value decomposition
$A=U\Sigma V^*$, and let $\tau\ge0$ be a declared threshold. The
**truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau$** is

$$ A_\tau^+ := V\Sigma_\tau^+U^*, $$

where $\Sigma_\tau^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is the transposed-shape
diagonal matrix whose $i$th diagonal entry is $\sigma_i^{-1}$ when
$\sigma_i>\tau$ and is $0$ when $\sigma_i\le\tau$; every off-diagonal entry is
$0$.

The threshold is part of the definition, exactly as in
[[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]]: changing
$\tau$ changes which singular directions are retained.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear map
between real or complex Hilbert spaces, with Hilbert adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$.
Write $\mathbb N_{>0}:=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. If $R(K)$ has finite dimension
$r\in\mathbb N$, put $J=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, interpreted as empty when $r=0$;
if $R(K)$ is infinite-dimensional, put $J=\mathbb N_{>0}$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values $s_j>0$ in nonincreasing order. Let
$(v_j)_{j\in J}$ and $(u_j)_{j\in J}$ be complete
orthonormal families in $N(K)^\perp$ and $\overline{R(K)}$, respectively,
with $Kv_j=s_ju_j$ and $K^*u_j=s_jv_j$. The empty sum is zero, finite $J$
uses a finite sum, and infinite $J$ uses the norm-convergent series whenever
the stated square-summability condition holds. Use inner products linear in the
first argument. Define the Picard sum
$$P_K(y):=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{|\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y|^2}{s_j^2},\qquad y\in Y.$$
Then:

1. The exact equation $Kx=y$ is solvable if and only if
   $y\perp N(K^*)$ and $P_K(y)<\infty$.

2. The domain of the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse is
   $$D(K^\dagger)=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp=\{y\in Y:P_K(y)<\infty\},$$
   and for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$,
   $$K^\dagger y=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y}{s_j}v_j.$$
   Thus the orthogonal component in $R(K)^\perp=N(K^*)$ is discarded by
   $K^\dagger$; exact range membership additionally requires that component
   to be zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. For every product-measurable kernel $a\in L^2(D\times D;\mathbb C)$, the formula $T_av(x)=\int_Da(x,y)v(y)dy$ defines a representative-independent complex-linear map $L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\|T_a\|\le\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D)}$. Consequently, under [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$,
$$\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\|G_k(\cdot-\cdot)q(\cdot)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\,\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$
For $|D|=0$ the operator is zero.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

For $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, extended by zero off $D$, set $G_k(z):=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ and $G_k(0):=0$, and let
$$K_{q,k}v(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \rho_k(q):=\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2(D)\to L^2(D)}.$$
The **small-norm contrast class** is
$$\mathcal U_{D,k}:=\{q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C):\rho_k(q)<1\}.$$
For $d\in S^2$, put $f_{k,d}(x):=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ on $D$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, let $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ denote the unique solution of $u=f_{k,d}+K_{q,k}u$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, define the exact far-field data family by
$$\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)u_{q,k,d}(y)\,dy,\qquad (\theta,d)\in S^2\times S^2.$$

For $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, define its first Born data by
$$\mathcal B_k h(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}h(y)e^{ikd\cdot y}\,dy=\frac1{4\pi}\widehat{h_0}\!\left(\frac{k}{2\pi}(\theta-d)\right),$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

where $h_0$ is the zero extension of $h$ to $\mathbb R^3$ and $\widehat g(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ for $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. No uniqueness or stability outside $\mathcal U_{D,k}$ is asserted.

**Inputs and admissible conditions.** Fix the domain $D$, wavenumber $k>0$, and library Fourier convention from the fixed-frequency data definition. Give nonempty finite lists of incident directions $d_1,\ldots,d_s\in S^2$ and observation directions $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\in S^2$. Give a finite measurable partition $D=\bigsqcup_{n=1}^N E_n$ with $|E_n|>0$, complex Born-data samples $y=(y_{ba})\in\mathbb C^{rs}$, a discrepancy threshold $\delta\ge0$, and an iteration budget $B\in\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. The sample frequency for pair $(\theta_b,d_a)$ is $\xi_{ba}:=k(\theta_b-d_a)/(2\pi)$. The declared finite discrete Born Fourier matrix $F\in\mathbb C^{rs\times N}$ has entries
$$F_{(b,a),n}:=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{E_n}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi_{ba}}\,dx.$$
For a piecewise-constant contrast $q_c:=\sum_{n=1}^N c_n1_{E_n}$, its sampled first Born data vector is exactly $Fc$.
The input also declares a reduced singular-value decomposition
$$Fc=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\sigma_j\langle c,v_j\rangle u_j\qquad(c\in\mathbb C^N),$$
where $p=\operatorname{rank}F$, the positive singular values $\sigma_j$ have orthonormal right vectors $v_j$ and orthonormal left vectors $u_j$, and the empty sum is used when $F=0$. Give a scalar filter $g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$ whose values at the $\sigma_j$ are finite and with $g(0)=0$. The threshold filter $g_\tau(\sigma)=1/\sigma$ for $\sigma>\tau$ and $g_\tau(\sigma)=0$ for $0\le\sigma\le\tau$ is the truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau\ge0$.

**Instructions and outputs.**

1. If $B=0$, return no estimate, no residual, and status **budget-exhausted**, with zero filter applications.
2. If $B\ge1$, form the coefficient estimate
   $$\widehat c:=\sum_{j:\sigma_j>0}g(\sigma_j)\langle y,u_j\rangle v_j,$$
   where $\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_\ell z_\ell\overline{w_\ell}$ is linear in its first argument. Return the piecewise-constant reconstruction $\widehat q:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\widehat c_n1_{E_n}$ after exactly one filter application.
3. Compute the finite data residual $R:=\|F\widehat c-y\|_2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\sum_\ell|z_\ell|^2)^{1/2}$. Return status **discrepancy** when $R\le\delta$, and **residual-above-threshold** when $R>\delta$; in either case also return $\widehat q$, $R$, and the application count $1$.

This procedure only defines one filtered finite-dimensional Born reconstruction and a residual status. The residual is not an exact-range test for an infinite-dimensional compact forward operator and does not establish a nonlinear solution, identifiability, stability, convergence, or correctness of the reconstructed contrast.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For each pair $(\theta_b,d_a)$ set $\xi_{ba}=k(\theta_b-d_a)/(2\pi)$ and define $F\in\mathbb C^{m\times N}$ by $F_{(b,a),n}=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{E_n}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi_{ba}}\,dx$.

Regard $F$ as the linear map $\mathbb C^{m+1}\to\mathbb C^m$. Its image is a subspace of dimension at most $m$ by [F5], so [F4] gives $\dim\ker F=(m+1)-\dim\operatorname{im}F\ge1$. Choose a nonzero $c=(c_n)_{n=1}^{m+1}\in\ker F$.

Define $h:=\sum_{n=1}^{m+1}c_n1_{E_n}$. Since at least one $c_n\ne0$ and each $E_n$ has positive measure, $h$ is a nonzero element of $L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$. By [F1] and [F2], $\mathcal B_kh(\theta_b,d_a)=(Fc)_{(b,a)}=0$ for every $1\le b\le r$, $1\le a\le s$. Thus the finite Born sample map has a nontrivial kernel.

For any scalar $t$, [F6] gives $\rho_k(th)\le C_D\|th\|_\infty=C_D|t|\|h\|_\infty$. The right-hand side tends to zero as $|t|\to0$, so choose $t\ne0$ small enough that $th\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$. Set $q:=th$. Linearity of $\mathcal B_k$ gives $\mathcal B_kq(\theta_b,d_a)=0$ for every acquisition pair while $q\ne0$. The vector $c$ is a nonzero coefficient representation of a contrast whose sampled first Born data are exactly those of zero.

For input $y=0$, any filter application in the algorithm gives $\widehat c=0$ by [F7]; the reconstruction is zero and $R=\|F(0)-0\|_2=0\le\delta$, so the status is discrepancy for every $\delta\ge0$ and positive budget. This status cannot distinguish the zero contrast from the nonzero contrast in step 3.1 within the finite Born model, and no statement about the exact nonlinear data was used.
